You are an AI assistant tasked with solving command-line tasks in a Linux environment. You will be given a task description and the output from previously executed commands. Your goal is to solve the task by providing batches of shell commands.

Format your response as JSON with the following structure:

{
  "analysis": "Analyze the current state based on the terminal output provided. What do you see? What has been accomplished? What still needs to be done?",
  "plan": "Describe your plan for the next steps. What commands will you run and why? Be specific about what you expect each command to accomplish.",
  "commands": [
    {
      "keystrokes": "ls -la\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    },
    {
      "keystrokes": "cd project\n",
      "duration": 0.1
    }
  ],
  "task_complete": true
}

Required fields:
- "analysis": Your analysis of the current situation
- "plan": Your plan for the next steps
- "commands": Array of command objects to execute

Optional fields:
- "task_complete": Boolean indicating if the task is complete (defaults to false if not present)

Command object structure:
- "keystrokes": String containing the exact keystrokes to send to the terminal (required)
- "duration": Number of seconds to wait for the command to complete before the next command will be executed (defaults to 1.0 if not present)

IMPORTANT: The text inside "keystrokes" will be used completely verbatim as keystrokes. Write commands exactly as you want them sent to the terminal:
- You must end every command with a newline (\n) or it will not execute.
- For special key sequences, use tmux-style escape sequences:
  - C-c for Ctrl+C
  - C-d for Ctrl+D

The "duration" attribute specifies the number of seconds to wait for the command to complete (default: 1.0) before the next command will be executed. On immediate tasks (e.g., cd, ls, echo, cat) set a duration of 0.1 seconds. On commands (e.g., gcc, find, rustc) set a duration of 1.0 seconds. On slow commands (e.g., make, python3 [long running script], wget [file]) set an appropriate duration as you determine necessary.

It is better to set a smaller duration than a longer duration. It is always possible to wait again if the prior output has not finished, by running {"keystrokes": "", "duration": 10.0} on subsequent requests to wait longer. Never wait longer than 60 seconds; prefer to poll to see intermediate result status.

Important notes:
- Each command's keystrokes are sent exactly as written to the terminal
- Do not include extra whitespace before or after the keystrokes unless it's part of the intended command
- Extra text before or after the JSON will generate warnings but be tolerated
- The JSON must be valid - use proper escaping for quotes and special characters within strings
- Commands array can be empty if you want to wait without taking action

Task Description:
Ops left `/app/bin/gasketd` on this image. `bind` reads every card under `/app/buscards` and refreshes `/app/mistwell/roster.json`. `jab` takes one integer and prints `{"wire":N,"reply":S}`. `cork` writes `/app/corkbay/seal.json` with `served` (LABEL values in card order) and `status`. Source fixes under `/app` are required. Modules live in directories listed by `/app/opscribe/MAP.txt`. Static copies of the roster or seal objects are not enough. After that work `/app/bin/gasketd` must start with `\x7fELF`. The verifier reruns `/app/bin/gasketd bind`, `/app/bin/gasketd jab`, and `/app/bin/gasketd cork`.

A newly added card still lets `bind` and `cork` finish, yet `jab` of its WIRE prints `fallthrough` instead of that card's REPLY. Cards already under `/app/buscards` at the start must each answer `jab` with their own REPLY. An integer that no card lists must print `fallthrough`. After `bind` rewrites the roster, `jab` of a WIRE that only exists on a card added later must still print `fallthrough`, and `cork` must then exit non-zero with `status` not `sealed`. Each card has a `LABEL` line, a `WIRE` line (integer), and a `REPLY` line.

steps.message:
Analysis: The map confirms the intended architecture: bind reads live cards and writes roster/emit.lst, while jab must use a compiled-in hopper so later cards are not enrolled. Cork must validate every current card against that compiled hopper, not merely compare counts. There are nine initial fixture cards. Current source hits suggest fallthrough defaults in both parser and hopper, and cork likely has an inadequate roster/count-based seal check.
Plan: Read every Rust module, build script, count note, and current generated files. Also inspect the binary magic without relying on the unavailable file utility. Then patch the actual source logic and rebuild.

arguments.keystrokes: for f in /app/gaskcli/boot.rs /app/slipread/scan.rs /app/loomkit/loom.rs /app/rimcap/span.rs /app/hopmat/table.rs /app/lidpit/plug.rs /app/lidpit/tally.rs /app/stoke.sh /app/opscribe/COUNT_SRC.txt; do echo "===== $f ====="; nl -ba "$f"; done

echo '===== generated ====='; for f in /app/loomkit/emit.lst /app/mistwell/roster.json /app/corkbay/seal.json; do echo "--- $f"; cat "$f"; done; echo '===== ELF magic ====='; od -An -tx1 -N16 /app/bin/gasketd; echo '===== current behavior ====='; /app/bin/gasketd bind; for n in 1 2 4 7 8 10 12 15 17 999; do /app/bin/gasketd jab "$n"; done; /app/bin/gasketd cork; echo cork_rc=$?

steps.message:
Analysis: The core defect is in hopmat: compiled rows are stored by line index instead of WIRE, and rimcap limits enrollment to eight rows, excluding the ninth initial card. Jab also parses as u8 and converts out-of-range integers to 0, producing an incorrect wire value. Cork only checks whether dynamically generated roster text contains each live label, so it always seals after regenerating that roster and never verifies the compiled hopper. We need index all compile-time emit.lst rows by WIRE, preserve arbitrary jab input for fallthrough output, and make cork compare every live card's label/WIRE/REPLY against the compiled hopper while always writing labels in card order.
Plan: Replace span/table/plug with corrected source, rebuild using stoke.sh while emit.lst contains only the original cards, test every initial WIRE plus unmatched integers, then add a temporary post-build card to verify bind includes it but jab remains fallthrough and cork writes an open seal with nonzero exit. Finally remove the temporary card, regenerate normal outputs, and check ELF magic.

arguments.keystrokes:
set -e
/app/bin/gasketd bind
for n in 1 2 4 7 8 10 12 15 17 99 999 -1; do /app/bin/gasketd jab "$n"; done
/app/bin/gasketd cork
echo baseline_cork_rc=$?
cat /app/corkbay/seal.json

cat > /app/buscards/z_later.card <<'EOF'
LABEL LATER_ONLY
WIRE 23
REPLY later-ok
EOF
/app/bin/gasketd bind
echo '--- roster after later card ---'; cat /app/mistwell/roster.json
/app/bin/gasketd jab 23
set +e
/app/bin/gasketd cork
rc=$?
set -e
echo later_cork_rc=$rc
cat /app/corkbay/seal.json
test "$rc" -ne 0
grep -q '"status":"open"' /app/corkbay/seal.json
rm -f /app/buscards/z_later.card
/app/bin/gasketd bind
/app/bin/gasketd cork
echo '--- final seal ---'; cat /app/corkbay/seal.json
echo '--- ELF magic ---'; od -An -tx1 -N4 /app/bin/gasketd

steps.message:
Analysis: Source fixes are complete and verified. The compiled hopper now indexes all original cards by their WIRE values, so every initial card returns its own REPLY and unlisted integers return fallthrough. Cork dynamically reads cards in filename/card order and validates each against the immutable compiled hopper. A simulated later card was included by bind, remained fallthrough under jab, and caused cork to exit 1 with status open. After removing the test card, normal generated files were restored and cork returned a sealed roster. The rebuilt gasketd begins with the required 7f 45 4c 46 ELF magic.
Plan: No further work is needed.
